Unit 2: Systems Control

HL curriculum overview and structured learning plan.

Introduction

How do machines manage chaos and control the physical world?

This unit focuses on two critical HL concepts: Concurrency (how OSs manage multiple tasks without crashing) and Control (how computers sense and change the physical world). You will master the logic of Feedback Loops and understand the dangers of Deadlock.

You'll start by looking at the Operating System's struggle to manage competing resources (Multitasking). Then you'll move to physical computing, defining the Input-Process-Output cycle of Sensors and Actuators, determining when to use Open-Loop vs Closed-Loop logic.

Multitasking & Deadlock

When multiple programs want the same resource, chaos can ensue.

  • Resource Contention: Processes fighting for CPU/Memory.
  • Deadlock: A standstill where Process A waits for B, and B waits for A. (The "Dining Philosophers" problem).
Control Systems Structure

Automated systems follow a strict Hardware-Software loop:

  1. Sensor: Detects physical data (Heat, Light).
  2. Transducer: Converts physics to electricity (ADC).
  3. Controller: The CPU/Logic that makes a decision.
  4. Actuator: The muscle that creates movement/change (Motor, Heater).
Feedback Loops

Does the system know if it succeeded?

  • Open-Loop: Input -> Process -> Output. (No checking. e.g., Cheap Toaster, Sprinkler).
  • Closed-Loop: Input -> Process -> Output -> Feedback -> Adjust. (Self-correcting. e.g., Thermostat, Cruise Control).
Key Terminology
TermDefinition
Multitasking The ability of an OS to execute more than one task simultaneously (via time-slicing).
Deadlock A situation where two or more processes are unable to proceed because each is waiting for the other to release a resource.
Sensor A device that detects or measures a physical property and records, indicates, or otherwise responds to it.
Actuator A component of a machine that is responsible for moving and controlling a mechanism or system.
Transducer A device that converts variations in a physical quantity (like pressure) into an electrical signal (or vice versa).
Feedback Information about the output of a system that is returned to the input to modify the next action.
Open-Loop System A control system where the output has no influence or effect on the control action.
Closed-Loop System A control system that uses feedback to maintain a desired output.
